title.en: How smkabir.com stays up: releases, pointers and a failover that is still on paper

description.en: How the site is served from a homelab: R2 releases, two pointers, what happens when things fail, and the failover Worker that is designed but not built yet.

children.text: This site is static files served by two small nginx pods in a homelab. That is a deliberately boring design, and it makes the interesting question easy to state: what keeps the site up when something breaks? This post is the honest answer, including the part that does not exist yet.

fields.title: What is built, and what is only planned

children.text: content that lives outside the container image, release and pointer handling in object storage, pods that follow the pointer, verified publishing, rollback, and two replicas on different hosts.

the failover Worker that would serve a copy of the site from object storage when the whole homelab is unreachable. Until it exists, a power cut or an internet outage takes the site down. Everything below says which side of that line it is on.

children.text: Nothing a visitor requests ever touches a database or a CMS. Pages are files. That is why the failure modes are few and the recovery is mostly "serve the previous files".
The content is not in the image
The container image holds nginx and a small sync program, and

A new post is therefore not a deployment. There is no commit to the cluster repository, no image build and no rollout. A publish uploads a folder and moves a pointer.
How a pod follows the pointer
Each pod runs a sidecar that does the same small loop every 60 seconds:

If any step fails, the previous release keeps serving. A visitor never sees a half-written site, and R2 being down means "keep what you have".

The failover that is not built yet

When the tunnel has no healthy connectors, Cloudflare answers with an error page, and its edge cache only helps on points of presence that happen to be warm. The design is a small Worker in front of the site:

fields.source:
direction: right

visitor: "Visitor" { shape: person }
worker: "Failover Worker (planned)"
origin: "Homelab origin"
r2: "R2: VERIFIED release" { shape: cylinder }

visitor -> worker
worker -> origin: "try first, 4 s timeout"
worker -> r2: "only on 5xx, tunnel error or timeout"
fields.alt: Planned design: a Cloudflare Worker receives every request. If the origin answers normally the response is passed through. If the origin returns a server error, a tunnel error or times out after four seconds, the Worker reads VERIFIED from R2 and serves that release, with an X-Served-From header.

children.text: goes straight to the origin; the Worker never invents a write.
It is the same bucket the pods read, so there is no second copy to keep in sync, and it never serves an unverified build.
The security headers come from one source file that renders both the nginx configuration and the Worker, so a mirrored response carries the same policy as an origin one.
, and an external uptime probe is meant to alert when it appears.
What still fails when the homelab is down:
publishing and previews. Reading, the resume, search and the feeds keep working, because they are files.
scale the deployment to zero through the cluster repository (Argo CD would undo a manual change within seconds), check the key pages and the header, then revert the commit.

It is on paper because the site only went live today and the failover is the next unit of work, not because it is hard. The release layout was chosen so that it is a small Worker and not a second system.
a manual workflow takes a build id, checks the release exists and is consistent, and rewrites
to it. The pods follow within a minute.
(the image): a tag is never moved. A fix is the next patch, and a rollback is reverting the commit that bumped the tag in the cluster repository.
What has been proven, and what has not
Proven in production in the last day:
uploads, pointer moves, pruning, and pods reading with a read-only token. The token that can write is a different token, held only by CI.
the content pipeline and the image release, including a vulnerability scan that stopped a release for a HIGH finding in a library the image did not need.
Argo CD sync, two ready pods on different hosts, the gateway route and the tunnel to the apex.
61 image checks (sidecar, nginx under the cluster's restrictions, redirects), 35 release-script checks, an end-to-end run of the real site through nginx, and unit tests.
Not proven: the failover Worker (it does not exist), a real power cut, and a sustained outage of the object store.
The wall CI hit on day one
The check in step 4 above failed for ten minutes with "last saw nothing". The site was serving the right release; the CI runner was being handed Cloudflare's

challenge page, because Bot Fight Mode treats a datacenter address as a bot. The fix was one switch. The more useful change was to the script: it now reports the HTTP status and the first bytes of what it received, instead of collapsing a challenge page, a 404 and a dead tunnel into the same word. A failure message that cannot distinguish its causes is a bug in the failure message.
It is the one gap in the table above.
In-cluster monitoring goes dark with the cluster; a probe on a Worker cron does not.
